title: Building Reliable Agentic Systems: Eno Reyes

summary: Eno Reyes presents lessons from Factory.ai's development of autonomous systems called Droids, which handle software development lifecycle tasks including code review, documentation, testing, and end-to-end coding. Each Droid has a separate cognitive architecture mapped to its task. He identifies three characteristics of agentic systems: planning (decisions about future actions), decision-making (criteria and algorithms for wide action spaces), and environmental grounding (reading and writing to external environments). For planning, he describes the pseudo common filter—passing intermediate reasoning through plan steps to converge toward consistent reasoning, while noting the risk of error propagation. He discusses subtask decomposition for finer control, model predictive control for adaptive replanning, and explicit plan criteria using hardcoded logic and few-shot examples, arguing this is practical for near-term value rather than waiting for AGI. For decision-making, he covers consensus mechanisms, explicit and analogical reasoning, fine-tuning for out-of-distribution decisions despite quality lock-in, and simulation using code execution and language agent tree search. For environmental grounding, he distinguishes between dedicated tools and custom AI-computer interfaces needed for novel workflows. When consistent tool chains are used repeatedly, building a custom interface streamlines those actions rather than relying on the agent to rediscover them each time. He then covers explicit feedback processing—parsing CI/CD logs to extract failing tests and provide explainers, and processing error trajectories from the agent's own self-reflection, since LLMs are better at listening to criticism instructions than self-criticizing organically. Bounded exploration balances gathering maximum context (leveraging long-context models like Gemini Pro 1.5 and Sonnet 3.5) against jumping into the problem, with the optimal balance being difficult to determine in advance and requiring significant evaluation. Finally, human guidance—deciding when to ask humans for interference or direction through careful UX and interaction design—can move systems from 30-40% reliability to 90-100%, representing a critical trade-off between autonomy and oversight.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: Agentic systems are characterized by planning, decision-making, and environmental grounding—each requiring distinct engineering approaches
The pseudo common filter passes intermediate reasoning through plan steps to converge toward consistent reasoning, but risks error propagation from early mistakes
Explicit plan criteria and hardcoded logic, while seemingly less generalizable, are practical for delivering near-term customer value rather than waiting for AGI
Consensus mechanisms improve decision accuracy but increase cost and latency if not parallelized
Simulation is particularly powerful in software development because code execution provides natural simulation capabilities
Custom AI-computer interfaces should streamline consistent multi-step tool chains rather than forcing agents to rediscover them each time
Explicit feedback processing—both for external logs and internal error trajectories—is critical because LLMs are better at following criticism instructions than self-criticizing
Bounded exploration balances context gathering against problem engagement, with the optimal balance requiring significant evaluation to determine

sections.title: Introduction to Factory.ai and Droids
sections.summary: Eno Reyes introduces Factory.ai's mission to bring autonomy to software engineering through Droids—autonomous systems for code review, documentation, testing, and end-to-end coding tasks. Each Droid has a separate cognitive architecture mapped to its task.

sections.title: Defining Agentic Systems
sections.summary: Defines agentic systems through three characteristics: planning (decisions about future actions), decision-making (criteria and algorithms for wide action spaces), and environmental grounding (reading and writing to external environments).

sections.title: Planning Techniques
sections.summary: Covers four planning techniques: pseudo common filter (passing intermediate reasoning through plan steps for convergence, with error propagation risk), subtask decomposition (finer control but more decisions), model predictive control (adaptive replanning from real-time feedback), and explicit plan criteria (hardcoded logic, instruction tuning, few-shot examples). Emphasizes pragmatic value of symbolic-era approaches.

sections.title: Decision-Making Approaches
sections.summary: Discusses consensus mechanisms (self-consistency, prompt ensembles, cluster sampling) for accuracy at higher cost; explicit and analogical reasoning (chain of thought, checklists, chain of density) to reduce decision complexity; fine-tuning for out-of-distribution decisions despite quality lock-in; and simulation using code execution and techniques like language agent tree search.

sections.title: Environmental Grounding and Tool Use
sections.summary: Introduces environmental grounding as tool use and AI-computer interfaces. Distinguishes between dedicated tools (calculators, sandboxed Python, Claude artifacts) and custom interfaces needed for workflows or trajectories not supported by existing tools.

sections.title: Custom Interfaces, Feedback Processing, Bounded Exploration, and Human Guidance
sections.summary: Continues environmental grounding with streamlining consistent tool chains into custom AI-computer interfaces. Covers explicit feedback processing for CI/CD logs and agent self-reflection error trajectories, noting LLMs follow criticism instructions better than self-criticizing. Discusses bounded exploration balancing context gathering with problem engagement using long-context models, requiring evaluation to tune. Concludes with human guidance through careful UX design that can raise reliability from 30-40% to 90-100%, trading autonomy for oversight. Mentions Factory.ai is hiring.

limitations: Pseudo common filter facilitates error propagation—a simple mistake early in a plan can lead to strong downstream effects
Subtask decomposition makes it harder for the system to decide what's right as more small tasks are introduced
Consensus mechanisms increase cost and may introduce longer inference wait times if not parallelized
Fine-tuning locks in system quality, losing the benefit of automatic improvement when new state-of-the-art models are released
Explicit plan criteria with hardcoded logic is difficult to build and scale
Simulation of decision-making is domain-specific and tricky
Finding the right balance of bounded exploration time is very difficult to know in advance and requires significant evaluation
LLMs are not great at criticizing their own actions but are good at listening to instructions to criticize themselves
Human guidance trades autonomy for oversight, requiring a deliberate trade-off
quantitativeClaims: Migrating even a small section of a codebase might require literally hundreds of steps in a process
Human guidance can take systems from 30 or 40% reliability to 90 or 100% reliability
